knowledge_type_note: A meta-record describing how this base handles the relationship between rules and their exceptions, and indexing the exceptions themselves.

history.notes: A meta-record about this base's own method; no external history.

engine_era_note: The engine era is why a good many of these exceptions are provable rather than arguable. Before tablebases, 'the rook belongs behind the passed pawn' could only be met with a counter-opinion; now it can be met with a proof that the same position is a draw one way and a loss in 63 the other.

preconditions: A principle is being applied to a position
false_positive_traps: An exception existing does not make a rule useless. Most of these rules are correct in the large majority of positions.
The absence of a recorded exception means this base has not found one, not that none exists.

typical_plans: Record the exception with the rule, never separately
Prefer a source's own statement of its condition over a later paraphrase
Where two principles conflict, record the resolution rather than dropping one

exceptions: Official rules of chess and proven results have no exceptions, and are typed so that the test suite does not demand any.
Mechanical tactical motifs have conditions rather than exceptions - a fork either exists on the board or does not.
limitations: Exceptions are only as complete as the research behind them; this base does not claim its lists are exhaustive and says so on individual concepts.
The index does not currently distinguish exceptions proven by measurement from those resting on authority, which is a known gap.

Counts in this record are stated as floors ('over N') rather than exact figures, because the base grows and an exact count written into prose silently becomes false. The live figures are in state/warnings_index.json and state/coverage.json.
misconceptions: That a principle with many exceptions is a bad principle. It may simply be a well-studied one.
That listing exceptions is hedging. It is the part that makes the rule applicable.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `an-exception-does-not-void-the-rule`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Here is a position where the most-quoted rule in rook endings fails: the defending rook is behind the passed pawn, exactly as Tarrasch prescribed, and Black is lost. A recorded exception to a recorded rule. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own first trap: "An exception existing does not make a rule useless. Most of these rules are correct in the large majority of positions." Finding this position does not license reporting the rule as unreliable, and the record exists to hold the two claims apart — 254 exceptions are recorded here precisely so that rules can be applied safely rather than abandoned. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN WIN in 63 for the attacker, with the defending rook obeying the rule. The API reports the position's features and makes no claim about rules at all, which is the only correct behaviour: `exceptions-to-rules` is a record ABOUT this base's other records rather than about boards, and a system that reported it would be reporting on itself. Read against the same position with that rook on f6, active on the sixth — the Vancura defence, a proven draw. One rook move between the rule failing and the rule being irrelevant, and neither of them is the rule being wrong.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 63 with the defending rook obeying Tarrasch's rule. The same position with that rook active on f6 is a PROVEN DRAW. One rook move between the rule failing and the rule being irrelevant, and neither is the rule being wrong.

by_level.beginner: Chess rules have exceptions, and knowing them is part of knowing the rule.
by_level.intermediate: A principle without its exceptions cannot be applied safely - the exception tells you the condition.
by_level.advanced: Three kinds: conditions the author stated and retelling dropped, proven counterexamples, and conflicts between two sound rules.
by_level.master: The third kind is the hard one, and is why every concept here carries an explicit conflicts list with a written resolution.

by_depth.short: Every principle here records where it fails.
by_depth.normal: A structural commitment of this base: every soft-typed concept must record its exceptions - over 250 so far - and the test suite fails the build if one does not. The exception is where the information is, because it shows the condition under which the rule applies.
by_depth.deep: A rule that holds everywhere tells you nothing about any particular position; what makes a principle usable is knowing its conditions, and conditions are only visible from the cases where the rule breaks. Three kinds are distinguished here. Conditions the original author stated and later retelling dropped - both worst-piece formulations are conditional, and Shereshevsky documents rook endings where his own first principle simply fails. Proven counterexamples, where a tablebase or controlled comparison settles the matter rather than an opinion. And conflicts between two sound principles pointing opposite ways, which is the hardest kind and is recorded structurally, each concept carrying a conflicts list with a written resolution so a caller meeting two applicable concepts has something better than a coin toss.

definition_short: Every principle here carries its exceptions - 254 recorded - because a rule without them cannot be applied safely.
definition_long:
A structural commitment of this knowledge base rather than a chess idea. Every concept typed as a principle, rule of thumb, guideline or positional concept must record where it fails, and the test suite enforces it: a soft-typed concept with no recorded exception fails the build.

THE REASON IS THAT THE EXCEPTION IS WHERE THE INFORMATION IS. A rule that holds everywhere tells you nothing about any particular position; what makes a principle usable is knowing the conditions under which it applies, and those conditions are only visible from the outside — from the cases where it breaks.

THE THREE KINDS this base distinguishes:
1. CONDITIONS THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR STATED and later retelling dropped. Anderssen's and Makogonov's worst-piece rules both carry explicit preconditions; Shereshevsky documents rook endings where his own first principle fails.
2. PROVEN COUNTEREXAMPLES, where a tablebase or a controlled engine comparison settles it. Tarrasch's rook rule, the check that loses, doubled pawns, the piece moved twice.
3. CONFLICTS BETWEEN PRINCIPLES, where two sound rules point opposite ways and the resolution is a further judgement — king safety against king activity, simplify against complicate when worse, material against activity.

THE THIRD KIND IS THE HARDEST and is recorded structurally: concepts carry an explicit conflicts list, each with a written resolution, so that a caller meeting two applicable concepts has something better than a coin toss.

All 254 exceptions are compiled into state/warnings_index.json alongside the misconceptions and detector traps.
